new_statements.quote: Comme toutes les langues de zone C, l'ebujá de Yambuli atteste deux tons de base: bas et haut. [...] Le dernier exemple indique que la tonalité haute est portée par la première syllabe du substantif et non nécessairement par le PN. La question de ton en cette langue pourrait donc plutôt provenir de sa confusion avec l'accent dynamique. [p. 209:] La langue des Mobango est bien un dialecte bujá, comme le montre notre étude (Motingea 1995) et l'affirment Van Bulck et Hackett (1956: 77)
new_statements.translation: Like all zone C languages, the Ebujá of Yambuli has two basic tones: low and high. [...] The last example shows that the high tone is carried by the first syllable of the noun and not necessarily by the nominal prefix. The tone question in this language might therefore rather stem from its confusion with dynamic accent (stress). [p. 209:] The language of the Mobango is indeed a Buja dialect, as our study (Motingea 1995) shows and as Van Bulck and Hackett (1956: 77) state.
new_statements.citation: Motingea Mangulu, André. 2003. Le parler bujá des Yambuli (bantou C.37). Annales Aequatoria 24: 205-261.
new_statements.locator: §2.3 Tonalité, pp. 221-222 (PDF pp. 216-217 of the volume; pp. 17-18 of the extracted article PDF); identity remark p. 209
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (57 pp., text layer) opens with the header "Annales Aequatoria 24(2003)205-261 / MOTINGEA MANGULU / LE PA[R]LER BUJÁ DES YAMBULI (Bantou C.37)"; the résumé says the data come from a Yambuli speaker from Kwanja near Ebonda (Secteur Molua, Territoire de Bumba), collected 1993 at Bamanya. All three quoted pieces are there verbatim at the stated locators: "Comme toutes les langues de zone C, l'ebujá de Yambuli atteste deux tons de base: bas et haut" (article p. 221 = PDF p. 17), "Le dernier exemple indique que la tonalité haute est portée par la première syllabe du substantif et non nécessairement par le PN. La question de ton en cette langue pourrait donc plutôt provenir de sa confusion a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two-tone (H/L) language with contour tones; no stress rule is given. The author notes that in prepositional and connective phrases a high tone lands on the first syllable of the noun rather than on its prefix, and speculates that this 'tone' may in fact be a dynamic (stress) accent. This is stated for the Yambuli Buja variety, which Motingea treats as the same language as Mobango/Babango; nothing is stated for Babango proper.
new_statements.exceptions: PB *HH nouns realised LH; infinitives (cl. 7) take low tone on the root; the author explicitly says a serious tonological study remains to be done (p. 222).
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms and phrase-level (prepositional/connective groups); the accent remark concerns the noun in a phrase. Applies to Buja des Yambuli (Budza, budz1238), not to Babango (baba1263) directly.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is from Motingea Mangulu 2003 on the Buja (Budza) of the Yambuli, Glottolog budz1238 (ISO bja), Bantu C.37. Motingea states (p. 209) that Mobango/Babango (baba1263, Guthrie C.44/C.441) is a Buja dialect on the evidence of his 1995 sketch, and Ethnologue likewise treats it as possibly a Budza dialect, but Glottolog keeps them as separate languages. The only description of Babango proper (Motingea 1995, AAP 41) could not be opened, so no first-hand statement for baba1263 itself was quoted; the Buja passage should not be entered under baba1263 without the 1995 sketch confirming the same pattern.

sources.note: §2.3 Tonalité (pp. 221-222): Yambuli Buja has two basic tones (L, H) plus rising/falling contours; PB *HH nouns have become LH; in prepositional/connective groups the H falls on the first syllable of the noun, and the author suggests the tone question may stem from confusion with 'l'accent dynamique' (stress). pp. 208-209: Mobango (=Babango) is 'bien un dialecte bujá' per his 1995 study. Describes Buja (budz1238), not Babango proper.

Stub: classification C.441, ~2,600 speakers; nothing on phonology.

sources.note: The only first-hand description of Babango (Ebango) proper; Motingea's C.40 sketches all carry a 'Tonalité' section (cf. his 2003 Buja and Egbuta sketches), so the tone/accent statement for this language is almost certainly here. AAP (1985-2000) was never digitized: not on KUPS, Cologne Digital Collections, archive.org or Google Books; the old institute site only had HTML tables of contents.
